summary:
Chicago was a major center of American filmmaking before Hollywood, with production studios and film exchanges that helped make movies widely available. Selig Polyscope began producing in the city in 1896, and Essanay Studios, founded in 1907, became one of the world’s largest film companies.

In 1909, the Motion Picture Patents Company restricted production and charged fees for films and equipment. Independent filmmakers resisted, and many moved west to avoid legal disputes and find better filming conditions. Chicago’s production industry declined as Hollywood grew, though the city remained a major theater and distribution center.

Film production returned in the 1980s. A 2009 Illinois tax credit covering 30% of production costs helped attract more projects. In 2011, Cinespace Chicago Film Studios opened in North Lawndale. It has hosted major films and television productions and contributed to local investment and job creation.
